title: Ang 730–750: the Gurus in Suhi
hookLine: the one whose head He guards, on ang 749
tomorrow: which red fades in a week, and which one holds?

lines: A HAND ON A HEAD IN A CROWD.
cards: Helmets, car seats, a parent's hand on a kid's head in a crowd: people guard heads. On ang 749, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: the one whose head you, Master, are over, how could that one suffer pain?
It sounds like a promise that nothing will go wrong. A gentle note for anyone listening with kids: today mentions the Guru's own death, without detail.

teach.b: These Suhi pages run through the Gurus in order, and ang 749 is Guru Arjan's. The hymn goes on, in paraphrase: you belong to the saints, and the saints are yours. Sikhs read 'guarded' in two ways.
The first stays close to the letter: God protects. Its best case: Sikhs pray Ardas for protection, before a journey, an exam, a surgery, and the Granth tells of devotees like Prahlad kept safe.
Why pray for protection if it isn't real? The second reading turns inward: the guarded head is a mind that can't be made to despair. Its best case is the writer himself.
Sikhs remember that Guru Arjan was tortured and put to death, and tradition says he met it accepting God's will as sweet. If 'guarded' meant nothing bad happens, his own life would answer no.

teach.h: ANOTHER: THE HELD MIND DOESN'T BREAK.
teach.b: So this reading says the guard is over the head, not the body: the one who is held doesn't break. The two readings ask different things of the hymn.

teach.h: A PROMISE IN THE DARK ROOM TOO.
teach.b: Both hear it as a real promise, and both say it in a dark room as well as a bright one.

how: Sikhs say Ardas for protection before journeys and at hard moments, and remember Guru Arjan's martyrdom; his Suhi hymn on ang 749 is sung in kirtan.

s: ang 749 promises that nothing bad will ever happen to the devout
Sikhs read 'guarded' more than one way; the writer himself was put to death, as Sikhs remember.
the hymn says the Master belongs to the saints, and the saints to him
you belong to the saints, and the saints are yours (ang 749).
Sikhs read 'guarded' only as physical safety
some read it as protection; others as a mind held steady, whatever happens.

games.q: a friend's mom recovers from surgery. at the celebration one aunt says it proves prayer protects. another aunt, whose husband didn't recover last year, goes quiet. what fits ang 749?
o: agree out loud: the hymn promises the faithful nothing bad happens.
say prayer doesn't really change anything, to be fair to her.
honor the recovery, and leave room: guarded can mean held, whatever comes.
games.why: Sikhs hear ang 749 as protection and as a mind held steady in harm. both readings can sit at the same table.

practice: Sit tall and rest both hands on the crown of your head, elbows wide, for a few slow breaths. Then let your hands come down to your lap, and notice whether the head still feels held. Stay with that feeling for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Ang 730. Where the Gurus' hymns in Suhi run on, to Guru Arjan's on ang 749: whose head you are over, how could they suffer?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sir, head; jis ke sir oopar toon suaamee, the one whose head you, Master, are over (ang 749).

carryVoice: Guarded: the hand is over the head, in the bright room and the dark one. Held, fifteen thirty-six.
